MM-LeJEPA: Correlated Gaussian Regularization for Multimodal Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures

Haowen Bai   Rui Gong   Meichen Liu   Ming-Xuan Weng   Bihan Wen   Kim-Hui Yap   Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Affiliation: Hyundai Motor Group Innovation Center Singapore (HMGICS) Email: haowen.bai@hotmail.com
Abstract

LeJEPA derives an isotropic Gaussian embedding target by minimizing, under its task assumptions, a Fisher information criterion that controls the task-averaged squared prediction bias. This enables unimodal self-supervised learning without reconstruction decoders, exponential-moving-average teachers, or contrastive negatives. However, its isotropic task prior does not account for the cross-modal structure of multimodal tasks that read shared content. We introduce MM-LeJEPA by extending LeJEPA’s task assumptions to multimodal learning. Specifically, we model multimodal tasks as strength-weighted combinations of components that read independent information from the two modalities and components that read the same content from both. Under explicit gradient-moment, correspondence, and symmetry assumptions, we derive a correlated Gaussian target that minimizes a weighted Fisher information functional under a fixed total variance constraint. An analytic transform adapts Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) to this target, yielding a two-term objective that combines distributional regularization with local-to-global prediction. The extension adds a single scalar hyperparameter, the target cross-modal correlation, and retains the simplicity of LeJEPA. On public audio-visual classification benchmarks, our results are competitive with representative open-source methods. Code will be released.

1 Introduction

Self-supervised learning aims to learn representations from unlabeled data that transfer to unknown downstream tasks. Across unimodal and multimodal settings, common approaches include contrastive learning (Chen et al., 2020b; He et al., 2020), self-distillation (Grill et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021), and masked reconstruction (He et al., 2022; Georgescu et al., 2023). Audio-visual methods combine these strategies with cross-modal alignment (Gong et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023), fine-grained synchronization (Araujo et al., 2025), and dedicated fusion mechanisms (Nagrani et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). While effective, these designs require choices about masking, alignment losses, and encoder sharing, without explicitly deriving a target joint embedding distribution from a prior over downstream tasks. This design and tuning burden makes it harder to develop a simple, reusable multimodal pretraining framework.

Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) provide a self-supervised learning framework that predicts one view’s representation from another rather than reconstructing inputs (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). This removes the need for an input-reconstruction decoder, but a collapse-prevention mechanism is still required (Assran et al., 2023; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025; Bardes et al., 2022). LeJEPA (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025) instead asks what distribution the embeddings should follow. It shows that, when nothing is known in advance about the downstream task and the total variance is fixed, an isotropic Gaussian, which spreads equally in all directions, minimizes a criterion that controls the average prediction bias of downstream probes. It then uses a lightweight regularizer, Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg), to pull the embeddings toward this distribution, which enables efficient representation learning without a reconstruction decoder, contrastive negatives, stop-gradient, or an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher.

LeJEPA was developed for a single modality, and its task prior treats all embedding directions alike. Multimodal learning, however, differs from unimodal learning in the structure of downstream tasks. With one encoder per modality, the joint embedding splits into an audio block and a video block. Audio and video may observe the same event, so part of the content captured by one encoder is also captured by the other, and a downstream task can read this shared content from both blocks at once. Applying LeJEPA’s isotropic Gaussian target directly to the concatenated audio-visual embedding penalizes exactly the cross-modal correlation that shared content induces, limiting the target’s suitability for tasks that read such content.

We therefore propose MM-LeJEPA, a multimodal extension of LeJEPA. The formulation applies to any pair of modalities; we develop and evaluate it for audio and video, the most common co-occurring pair. We single out a class of tasks specific to multimodal learning, those that read shared content from both modalities, and model downstream tasks as strength-weighted combinations of independent-information and shared-content components. Under assumptions that, like LeJEPA’s, favor no feature direction within each modality, this yields a task prior suited to multimodal learning. The optimal embedding distribution under this prior is a correlated Gaussian: each modality remains an isotropic Gaussian, while the audio and video embeddings are correlated through one coefficient ρ\rho. The target reduces to LeJEPA’s isotropic Gaussian when shared content is absent, and its correlation grows with the contribution of shared content. Our contributions are:

  • •

    MM-LeJEPA extends LeJEPA to multimodal learning by accounting for both independent and shared information in its task prior. The objective retains two terms, and the distributional extension introduces only one target-correlation parameter ρ\rho, without requiring reconstruction decoders, EMA teachers, or contrastive negatives.

  • •

    We model independent-information and shared-content task components and derive a correlated Gaussian that minimizes the resulting weighted Fisher information functional under explicit assumptions and a total-variance constraint. A fixed whitening transform makes this target compatible with SIGReg, and local-to-global prediction preserves content.

  • •

    Comparisons with open-source methods on public audio-visual benchmarks show competitive attentive-probing results and fine-tuning performance.

2 Related Work

2.1 Audio-visual self-supervised pretraining

Paired audio and video provide natural self-supervision: early work transferred visual knowledge to audio (Aytar et al., 2016), predicted audio-image correspondence (Arandjelović & Zisserman, 2017; Arandjelović & Zisserman, 2018) or temporal synchronization (Korbar et al., 2018; Owens & Efros, 2018), and later work added cross-view contrastive learning (Tian et al., 2020), cross-modal clustering supervision (Alwassel et al., 2020) and refined positive pairs (Morgado et al., 2021b; Morgado et al., 2021a; Patrick et al., 2021). Recent methods reconstruct masked audio-visual content: Audiovisual MAE reconstructs both modalities with a shared decoder, trained from scratch on the target dataset (Georgescu et al., 2023); CAV-MAE and MAViL add cross-modal contrastive learning, and MAViL also adds a self-training stage with targets from a teacher that sees the complete input (Gong et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023); CAV-MAE Sync aligns individual audio segments with video frames (Araujo et al., 2025). Others vary the architecture or enforce augmentation consistency: MBT fuses modalities through a few bottleneck tokens (Nagrani et al., 2021), AVSiam shares one Vision Transformer across modalities (Lin & Bertasius, 2024), and EquiAV models equivariance to input augmentations (Kim et al., 2024).

These methods encode cross-modal relationships through reconstruction, alignment or architectural choices, without deriving a target joint embedding distribution from a prior over downstream tasks. MM-LeJEPA specifies such a distribution and exposes its cross-modal correlation as a scalar ρ\rho, and needs no reconstruction decoder, contrastive negatives, EMA teacher or self-training stage.

2.2 Joint-embedding predictive architectures and LeJEPA

JEPAs predict one view’s embedding from another’s instead of reconstructing inputs (LeCun, 2022), so the encoder can discard unpredictable low-level detail. I-JEPA applies this to image blocks (Assran et al., 2023), V-JEPA and V-JEPA 2 to video (Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025), A-JEPA to audio (Fei et al., 2023), data2vec to speech, vision and language (Baevski et al., 2022), and iBOT learns an online tokenizer by self-distillation (Zhou et al., 2022). Since latent prediction admits the constant solution, these methods prevent collapse with stop-gradient and a moving-average teacher, as does MJEPA for intra- and cross-modal audio-visual prediction with a modality-shared encoder (Teotia et al., 2026). A parallel line uses explicit geometric constraints instead: contrastive repulsion (Chen et al., 2020b; He et al., 2020), cross-correlation or variance–covariance penalties (Zbontar et al., 2021; Bardes et al., 2022), alignment and uniformity on the hypersphere (Wang & Isola, 2020), and batch-estimated whitening (Ermolov et al., 2021).

LeJEPA prevents collapse by using SIGReg to regularize embeddings toward an isotropic Gaussian target (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025). This target follows from its analysis of task-averaged integrated squared bias under a task-gradient prior and regularity assumptions. LeVJEPA extends global–local invariance with SIGReg to video (Kuhn et al., 2026), AV-JEPA combines early fusion and modality dropout with the LeJEPA objective without an EMA teacher (Robson et al., 2026), and Le MuMo JEPA pairs RGB images with depth or thermal images through learnable fusion tokens while keeping the isotropic target (Cornelissen et al., 2026).

Rather than applying LeJEPA’s isotropic target unchanged, MM-LeJEPA derives a joint target from explicit assumptions about multimodal tasks: a shared-content component adds cross-modal structure to the second moment of the task gradient, and minimizing the resulting weighted Fisher information functional under a fixed total variance yields a correlated Gaussian target.

3 Method

Overview.

We follow LeJEPA’s distribution-design approach. Section 3.1 expresses it in a matrix-weighted form: a prior over downstream tasks fixes the second moment WW of the task gradient and yields the weighted Fisher functional JWJ_{W} that controls the bias of nonlinear probes, and minimizing JWJ_{W} under a fixed total variance yields the target embedding distribution. Section 3.2 derives WW from a multimodal task prior with a shared-content component, Section 3.3 minimizes the corresponding functional JWAVJ_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}} and obtains a correlated Gaussian target with a single parameter ρ\rho, and Section 3.4 enforces this target with SIGReg through a fixed whitening transform.

3.1 Preliminaries: LeJEPA’s assumptions about downstream tasks

Let 𝐙∈ℝN×K\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K} denote the matrix of NN embeddings produced by the encoder fθf_{\theta} from the inputs 𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{n}, where each row is a KK-dimensional embedding fθ​(𝐱n)⊤f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{n})^{\top}. We write pzp_{z} for the distribution of a single embedding 𝐳=fθ​(𝐱)\mathbf{z}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}). As in LeJEPA, pzp_{z} has zero mean and covariance Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0. The unknown labels of a downstream task are given by a target function η:ℝK→ℝ\eta:\mathbb{R}^{K}\to\mathbb{R}, with gradient ∇η​(𝐪)\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q}) at a query point 𝐪\mathbf{q}. This gradient describes the task’s local sensitivity along each embedding direction.

LeJEPA’s objective.

We express LeJEPA’s probe-bias analysis in a matrix-weighted form for task-averaged integrated squared bias (ISB). The analysis yields a quantity that depends on the embedding distribution and controls the ISB; minimizing it under the variance constraint gives the optimal distribution for this criterion. We first obtain this quantity, JWJ_{W}.

We first consider a task prior fixed independently of the candidate representation distributions, and assume the task gradient has a zero first moment and a common positive-definite second moment:

𝔼η[∇η(𝐪)]=0,𝔼η[∇η(𝐪)∇η(𝐪)⊤]=W≻0.\mathbb{E}_{\eta}\!\left[\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})\right]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\eta}\!\left[\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})^{\top}\right]=W\succ 0. (1)

Both conditions hold with the same WW for almost every 𝐪\mathbf{q}, with finite second moments; a zero mean indicates no preferred signed gradient direction, and the form of WW is left unspecified.

Let ℐ(pz):=𝔼𝐳∼pz[∇logpz(𝐳)∇logpz(𝐳)⊤]\mathcal{I}(p_{z}):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{z}}\!\left[\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{z})\,\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{z})^{\top}\right] be the Fisher information matrix. We use the weighted Fisher information functional below as a surrogate objective, with weights given by the task-gradient second moment WW; the second equality is proved in Appendix D.1:

JW​(pz):=∫ℝK(∇log⁡pz​(𝐳))⊤​W​(∇log⁡pz​(𝐳))​pz​(𝐳)​𝑑𝐳=tr⁡(W​ℐ​(pz)).J_{W}(p_{z}):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{K}}\left(\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{z})\right)^{\top}W\left(\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{z})\right)p_{z}(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(W\mathcal{I}(p_{z})\right). (2)

Following LeJEPA’s task setting and derivations, we consider two nonlinear probes: radius-based kk-NN (Cover & Hart, 1967) and the Nadaraya–Watson kernel probe (Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1964). Under the task-gradient and curvature moment assumptions and each probe’s regularity conditions, this functional controls their task-averaged ISB over queries 𝐪∼pz\mathbf{q}\sim p_{z}:

ISBk​NN=ck​NN,0+ck​NN,1​JW​(pz)+εk​NN,ISBker≤cker,0+cker,1​JW​(pz)+εker.\mathrm{ISB}_{k\mathrm{NN}}={c_{k\mathrm{NN},0}+c_{k\mathrm{NN},1}}\,J_{W}(p_{z})+\varepsilon_{k\mathrm{NN}},\qquad\mathrm{ISB}_{\mathrm{ker}}\leq c_{\mathrm{ker},0}+c_{\mathrm{ker},1}\,J_{W}(p_{z})+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ker}}. (3)

Both relations are derived in Appendix D.2. Each cc is a nonnegative constant independent of the candidate distribution’s shape, and each ε\varepsilon is an infinitesimal term; the distribution-dependent design term is JW​(pz)J_{W}(p_{z}).

Optimizing the control quantity JWJ_{W}.

Following LeJEPA’s distribution-design strategy, we minimize JW​(pz)J_{W}(p_{z}), which controls the task-averaged ISB, to obtain the optimal shape of the embedding distribution.

LeJEPA further assumes an isotropic second moment to model unknown downstream tasks without favoring any gradient direction. That is, WW in Eq. (1) is taken to be W=τg2​IKW=\tau_{g}^{2}I_{K} with 0<τg2<∞0<\tau_{g}^{2}<\infty.

Under this isotropic prior, Eq. (2) reduces to JW​(pz)=τg2​tr⁡ℐ⁡(pz)=τg2​J​(pz)J_{W}(p_{z})=\tau_{g}^{2}\operatorname{tr}\mathcal{I}(p_{z})=\tau_{g}^{2}J(p_{z}), where J⁡(pz):=tr⁡ℐ⁡(pz)=∫ℝK‖∇log⁡pz​(𝐳)‖2​pz​(𝐳)​𝑑𝐳J(p_{z}):=\operatorname{tr}\mathcal{I}(p_{z})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{K}}\|\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{z})\|^{2}p_{z}(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z} is the Fisher information functional of LeJEPA. LeJEPA optimizes over all distributions of 𝐳\mathbf{z} subject to a fixed total-variance constraint. Taking that constraint to be tr⁡(Σ)=K\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=K, i.e. unit average coordinate variance,

JW​(pz)=τg2​J​(pz)≥τg2​tr⁡(Σ−1)≥τg2​K.J_{W}(p_{z})=\tau_{g}^{2}J(p_{z})\;\geq\;\tau_{g}^{2}\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Sigma^{-1}\right)\;\geq\;\tau_{g}^{2}K. (4)

The two inequalities hold with equality if and only if pz=𝒩⁡(0,Σ)p_{z}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) and Σ=IK\Sigma=I_{K}, respectively; proof references for both inequalities and their equality conditions are given in Appendix D.3. Therefore, when JW​(pz)J_{W}(p_{z}) attains its minimum, pzp_{z} must satisfy both conditions, i.e., pz∗=𝒩⁡(0,IK)p_{z}^{*}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{K}).

The constraint in LeJEPA.

LeJEPA then constrains the embeddings with SIGReg, which drives the distribution to the standard Gaussian by matching random one-dimensional projections with a univariate normality test (Epps & Pulley, 1983). A single weight combines this distributional term with a prediction loss that pulls an input’s crop embeddings toward the mean embedding of its global crops, similar to the local-to-global correspondence in multi-crop training (Caron et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021). The resulting objective needs no reconstruction decoder, EMA teacher, or contrastive negatives: prediction preserves content, while SIGReg constrains the distribution.

Summary.

The target is thus governed by the second moment WW of the task prior: an isotropic WW gives an isotropic Gaussian, and a prior that couples two modalities changes the target only through WW, which the next subsections derive for multimodal tasks.

3.2 Multimodal task prior and the second moment of the joint task gradient

Figure 1 summarizes MM-LeJEPA from view construction to prediction and regularization.

From unimodal to multimodal tasks.

Section 3.1 shows that the target is fixed by the second moment WW of the task gradient, and LeJEPA takes WW isotropic because nothing is known about the task. With two modalities this choice is no longer neutral. The coordinates of the joint embedding come from two encoders, and audio and video often observe the same event, so a task that reads such shared content has gradients on the two sides that vary together; its second moment has cross-modal blocks that an isotropic WW sets to zero. LeJEPA’s isotropic target would therefore penalize exactly this correlation. We keep LeJEPA’s route, a task prior that fixes WW and the induced functional JWJ_{W}, and change only the prior so that WW carries the cross-modal structure of shared-content tasks.

Multimodal task prior.

As in LeJEPA, we minimize JWJ_{W} to control the ISB of Eq. (3). This section constructs the task-prior second moment WAVW_{\mathrm{AV}} for multimodal tasks. Multimodal tasks differ from unimodal ones in that some read the same information from both modalities at once.

For an audio-visual task, let the projected audio and video embeddings be 𝐞a,𝐞v∈ℝd\mathbf{e}_{a},\mathbf{e}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and their joint embedding be 𝐳=[𝐞a;𝐞v]∈ℝ2​d\mathbf{z}=[\mathbf{e}_{a};\mathbf{e}_{v}]\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}. At a fixed query point 𝐪\mathbf{q}, we split the task gradient into blocks with respect to 𝐞a\mathbf{e}_{a} and 𝐞v\mathbf{e}_{v}:

∇η​(𝐪)=[∇aη⊤,∇vη⊤]⊤,∇aη,∇vη∈ℝd.\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})=\left[\nabla_{a}\eta^{\top},\ \nabla_{v}\eta^{\top}\right]^{\top},\qquad\nabla_{a}\eta,\nabla_{v}\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (5)

Audio and video can provide different observations of the same content. We model a downstream task through independent-information and shared-content components, combining their gradient contributions with different strengths:

∇η=1−π∇ηind+π∇ηsame,0≤π<1.\nabla\eta=\sqrt{1-\pi}\,\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}+\sqrt{\pi}\,\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{same}},\qquad 0\leq\pi<1. (6)

Here ηind\eta_{\mathrm{ind}} reads independent information from the two modalities and ηsame\eta_{\mathrm{same}} reads the same content from both; the task prior is their combination, and π\pi is a normalized squared-amplitude weight.

For example, identifying a guitar from its sound and image reads shared content, whereas recognizing background speech from audio and the shirt color from video reads independent information.

Fixed correspondence of multimodal content.

The same content can be read out from both audio and video, but the directions and scales in which the two encoders represent it are arbitrary, and this arbitrariness carries over to the task distribution through the relation between the audio and video gradients of a shared-content task. To derive a target from the task prior, we therefore assume that this relation is fixed by how the two encoders represent the content and does not depend on the task; a single change of coordinates then aligns the two sides so that the gradient of shared content is the same in both modalities, and the task prior is formulated in terms of this fixed relation.

Assumption 1 (fixed correspondence of shared content).

There exist a fixed orthogonal R∈O⁡(d)R\in O(d) and a fixed positive diagonal Λ≻0\Lambda\succ 0, independent of the task and the query point, such that

∇vηsame=Λ​R​∇aηsame.\nabla_{v}\eta_{\mathrm{same}}=\Lambda R\,\nabla_{a}\eta_{\mathrm{same}}. (7)

Change of coordinates for a simpler form.

An invertible change of coordinates leaves every task readout unchanged and maps each candidate embedding distribution to exactly one distribution in the new coordinates. We formulate the distribution-design problem in the common coordinates defined below. In Assumption 1, RR describes the directional correspondence of shared-content readouts, while Λ\Lambda accounts for their coordinate-wise scaling. We absorb these fixed differences into aligned video coordinates 𝐞~v=R⊤​Λ​𝐞v\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{v}=R^{\top}\Lambda\mathbf{e}_{v}. The same shared-content readout, expressed in (𝐞a,𝐞~v)(\mathbf{e}_{a},\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{v}), then satisfies

∇𝐞~vηsame=∇aηsame.\nabla_{\widetilde{\mathbf{e}}_{v}}\eta_{\mathrm{same}}=\nabla_{a}\eta_{\mathrm{same}}. (8)

All subsequent moments, probe calculations and variance constraints are defined in these common coordinates, and we henceforth write 𝐞v\mathbf{e}_{v} for the aligned video coordinates; no per-task gradient correspondence is required for the independent-information component.

General assumptions on multimodal tasks.

As in LeJEPA, the downstream task is not known in advance, so we place no preference on the direction of the task gradient: in the common coordinates, the gradient of each component has zero mean and an isotropic second moment within each modality, with the same strength on the two sides so that no modality is preferred, and the two components read mutually independent information. The shared-content component adds cross-modal structure under the correspondence and independence assumptions.

Assumption 2 (moments and independence of task gradients).

For m,m′∈{a,v}m,m^{\prime}\in\{a,v\}, the independent-information component has independent modality gradients with

𝔼η​[∇mηind]=0,𝔼η​[∇mηind​∇m′ηind⊤]=δm​m′​τind2​Id,\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\nabla_{m}\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\nabla_{m}\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}\,\nabla_{m^{\prime}}\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}^{\top}]=\delta_{mm^{\prime}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ind}}^{2}I_{d}, (9)

where δm​m′\delta_{mm^{\prime}} is the Kronecker delta. The shared-content component has gradients that coincide in the common coordinates by Eq. (8), with

𝔼η​[∇mηsame]=0,𝔼η​[∇mηsame​∇m′ηsame⊤]=τsame2​Id.\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\nabla_{m}\eta_{\mathrm{same}}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\nabla_{m}\eta_{\mathrm{same}}\,\nabla_{m^{\prime}}\eta_{\mathrm{same}}^{\top}]=\tau_{\mathrm{same}}^{2}I_{d}. (10)

The two components are independent, hence 𝔼η[∇ηind∇ηsame⊤]=0\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{same}}^{\top}]=0. Here 0<τind2,τsame2<∞0<\tau_{\mathrm{ind}}^{2},\tau_{\mathrm{same}}^{2}<\infty.

Under the assumptions above, let WAV:=𝔼η[∇η∇η⊤]W_{\mathrm{AV}}:=\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\nabla\eta\nabla\eta^{\top}] be the joint task-gradient second moment.

Proposition 1.

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, the component gradient second moments are

Wind=τind2​[Id00Id],Wsame=τsame2​[IdIdIdId],W_{\mathrm{ind}}=\tau_{\mathrm{ind}}^{2}\begin{bmatrix}I_{d}&0\\ 0&I_{d}\end{bmatrix},\qquad W_{\mathrm{same}}=\tau_{\mathrm{same}}^{2}\begin{bmatrix}I_{d}&I_{d}\\ I_{d}&I_{d}\end{bmatrix}, (11)

so that the second moment of the joint task gradient is

WAV=(1−π)​Wind+π​Wsame=τAV2​[Idω​Idω​IdId],W_{\mathrm{AV}}=(1-\pi)W_{\mathrm{ind}}+\pi W_{\mathrm{same}}=\tau_{\mathrm{AV}}^{2}\begin{bmatrix}I_{d}&\omega I_{d}\\ \omega I_{d}&I_{d}\end{bmatrix}, (12)

with τAV2=(1−π)​τind2+π​τsame2>0\tau_{\mathrm{AV}}^{2}=(1-\pi)\tau_{\mathrm{ind}}^{2}+\pi\tau_{\mathrm{same}}^{2}>0 and ω=π​τsame2/τAV2∈[0,1)\omega=\pi\tau_{\mathrm{same}}^{2}/\tau_{\mathrm{AV}}^{2}\in[0,1).

The second-moment expression is derived in Appendix D.4. At ω=0\omega=0, WAV=τAV2​I2​dW_{\mathrm{AV}}=\tau_{\mathrm{AV}}^{2}I_{2d} recovers LeJEPA’s isotropic second-moment assumption over the full embedding space in Section 3.1. This isotropic prior ignores cross-modal coupling, whereas ω\omega controls the contribution of shared-content components to the gradient second moment.

Summary.

This section derived the task prior for multimodal tasks and its second moment WAVW_{\mathrm{AV}}. As in LeJEPA, the next section minimizes the Fisher information functional JWAVJ_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}} induced by this prior under the total-variance constraint to obtain the optimal embedding distribution.

3.3 The optimal joint target distribution

With WAVW_{\mathrm{AV}} in hand, this section solves for the optimal distribution under the multimodal prior: among all embedding distributions with a fixed total variance, find the one that minimizes JWAVJ_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}}, the quantity that controls the probes’ bias.

Optimizing the control quantity JWAVJ_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}}.

With WAVW_{\mathrm{AV}} from Proposition 1, the weighted Fisher information functional of Eq. (2) reads JWAV​(pz)=tr⁡(WAV​ℐ​(pz))J_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}}(p_{z})=\operatorname{tr}(W_{\mathrm{AV}}\mathcal{I}(p_{z})); we minimize it under a fixed total-variance constraint to obtain the optimal shape of the embedding distribution.

Proposition 2.

Let pzp_{z} be an everywhere-positive density on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} with zero mean and covariance Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0. Assume pz∈C3p_{z}\in C^{3} with bounded derivatives up to order three, and assume finite Fisher information and covariance. Then

JWAV​(pz)≥tr⁡(WAV​Σ−1),J_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}}(p_{z})\ \geq\ \operatorname{tr}\!\left(W_{\mathrm{AV}}\Sigma^{-1}\right), (13)

and, when WAV≻0W_{\mathrm{AV}}\succ 0, equality holds if and only if pz=𝒩⁡(0,Σ)p_{z}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma). The proof is given in Appendix D.5.

As in LeJEPA, we impose the total-variance constraint tr⁡(Σ)=2​d\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=2d, which only fixes the overall scale; the optimal covariance then takes the form below, with unit variance per coordinate.

Proposition 3.

Let WAVW_{\mathrm{AV}} have the form in Eq. (12), with ω∈[0,1)\omega\in[0,1). Under the total-variance constraint above, the unique minimizer of tr⁡(WAV​Σ−1)\operatorname{tr}(W_{\mathrm{AV}}\Sigma^{-1}) over Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0 is

Σ∗​(ρ)=[Idρ​Idρ​IdId],ρ=ω1+1−ω2.\Sigma^{*}(\rho)=\begin{bmatrix}I_{d}&\rho I_{d}\\ \rho I_{d}&I_{d}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\rho=\frac{\omega}{1+\sqrt{1-\omega^{2}}}. (14)

The covariance and correlation formulas are derived in Appendix D.6.

The optimal distribution shape for multimodal tasks.

Propositions 2 and 3 show that, under the total-variance constraint, 𝒩​(0,Σ∗​(ρ))\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{*}(\rho)) uniquely minimizes JWAV​(pz)J_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}}(p_{z}); we adopt it as our target embedding distribution. The task-prior parameters π\pi, τind2\tau_{\mathrm{ind}}^{2} and τsame2\tau_{\mathrm{same}}^{2} are unknown before pretraining, so we retain this correlated Gaussian family and treat ρ\rho as an empirical hyperparameter.

3.4 Enforcing the target distribution with SIGReg

Constraining the transformed embedding with SIGReg.

SIGReg regularizes embeddings toward a standard Gaussian (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025). To adapt it to our correlated target, we first apply a fixed linear whitening transform that maps the target covariance to the identity (Kessy et al., 2018). We then apply SIGReg to the transformed embeddings. For the joint projection 𝐳=[𝐞a;𝐞v]\mathbf{z}=[\mathbf{e}_{a};\mathbf{e}_{v}] and |ρ|<1|\rho|<1, the transform is

Tρ​𝐳=[𝐞a+𝐞v2​(1+ρ);𝐞a−𝐞v2​(1−ρ)].T_{\rho}\mathbf{z}=\left[\frac{\mathbf{e}_{a}+\mathbf{e}_{v}}{\sqrt{2(1+\rho)}}\ ;\ \frac{\mathbf{e}_{a}-\mathbf{e}_{v}}{\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}}\right]. (15)

Since TρT_{\rho} is invertible, Tρ​𝐳∼𝒩⁡(0,I2​d)T_{\rho}\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{2d}) if and only if 𝐳∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ∗​(ρ))\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^{*}(\rho)), so constraining the transformed embedding to a standard Gaussian enforces Eq. (14).

Our objective follows the prediction and regularization structure of LeJEPA. Following its view-counting convention, each audio-visual sample produces one global embedding 𝐠\mathbf{g} and VlV_{l} local embeddings 𝐳1,…,𝐳Vl\mathbf{z}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{z}_{V_{l}}, one per audio window or video frame, and every local embedding predicts the global embedding. The prediction term is the coordinate-wise mean squared error:

ℒpred=1d​Vl​∑i=1Vl‖𝐳i−𝐠‖2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{1}{dV_{l}}\sum_{i=1}^{V_{l}}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{g}\right\|^{2}. (16)

The distributional term ℒSIGReg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}} applies SIGReg with the target derived above to the global and to the local embeddings. The overall objective is

ℒ=(1−λ)​ℒpred+λ​ℒSIGReg,λ∈[0,1].\mathcal{L}=(1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}},\qquad\lambda\in[0,1]. (17)

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental setup

We pretrain on AudioSet without using its class labels (Gemmeke et al., 2017). Because some videos are no longer available, our copies are smaller than the official lists; Appendix A gives the exact counts. We evaluate on VGGSound (VGG), a 309-class single-label classification benchmark (Chen et al., 2020a), and on the balanced and full training subsets of AudioSet (527 labels), denoted AudioSet-20K (AS-20K) and AudioSet-2M. We report top-1 accuracy for VGGSound and mean average precision (mAP) for AudioSet, in percent; A, V and A-V denote audio-only, video-only and audio-visual inputs.

Our encoder follows the ViT-B/16 configuration, with modality-specific patch embeddings and eleven modality-specific transformer blocks followed by a shared transformer block (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Gong et al., 2023). Audio is represented by a 128-bin log-mel spectrogram with 1,024 time positions, and video frames are resized to 224×224224\times 224. A shared projection head maps the 768-dimensional backbone features to 128 dimensions. The reference configuration uses one jointly encoded global audio-visual view, seven local audio windows, and nine video-frame views sampled from a sixteen-frame pool. The encoder is initialized from ImageNet-MAE weights (He et al., 2022). Pretraining runs for 30 epochs with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) at learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} and batch size 256, with λ=0.05\lambda=0.05 and target correlation ρ=0.8\rho=0.8.

4.2 Frozen-backbone probing

Attentive probing trains an attention-pooling head (Chen et al., 2024; Bardes et al., 2024) on the frozen encoder for 20 epochs, and linear probing trains a single linear layer on mean-pooled frozen features. Baselines use their released weights under the same code. Table 1 compares the frozen features. With attentive probing, MM-LeJEPA is best in all six cells, ahead of the strongest baseline in each column by 1.1–2.3 points on VGGSound and by 0.5–2.3 points on AudioSet-20K. With linear probing it is best in four of the six cells, including both audio-visual cells (46.9 vs. 46.0 and 36.3 vs. 35.1), while AVSiam, which shares one transformer across modalities, has the strongest video-only features. This is the setting the distributional target is designed for: the encoder is not adapted, so the scores reflect the embedding distribution itself.

4.3 Fine-tuning on three datasets

Fine-tuning attaches a classification head and uses AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) (learning rate 10−410^{-4}) for 10 epochs on VGGSound, Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) (learning rate 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4}) for 15 on AudioSet-20K and Adam (learning rate 10−510^{-5}) for 15 on AudioSet-2M, with cosine schedules. Table 2 reports the fine-tuning results. MM-LeJEPA performs on par with the best open-source methods on all three datasets, without contrastive negatives, EMA teacher or self-training.

VGGSounder.

VGGSounder (Zverev et al., 2025) re-annotates the VGGSound test set with multi-label, modality-specific labels. Following its protocol, we evaluate the VGGSound fine-tuned models on the background-music-free subset with the v1.0 labels, take the top-1 prediction, and report subset accuracy, F1 and hit rate separately for audio, visual and audio-visual inputs (Table 3; Appendix C reports the full test set). Baseline results are taken from the benchmark paper (Zverev et al., 2025) (arXiv v5, v1.0 labels). MM-LeJEPA obtains the highest score in all nine columns.

4.4 Sensitivity to target correlation, regularization weight and batch size

Table 7 varies the target correlation ρ\rho. Moving it away from the reference degrades every score: mildly for ρ=0.2\rho=0.2 (by at most 0.7), clearly for ρ=0.99\rho=0.99 (by 2.1–4.1 points), and sharply for LeJEPA’s isotropic target ρ=0\rho=0, whose attentive-probing scores fall by 8.8 and 9.8; Appendix B visualizes the effect of ρ\rho on the embeddings. Tables 5 and 5 vary the regularization weight λ\lambda and the batch size around the reference configuration. With λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 the scores stay within 0.7 of the reference, whereas λ=0.2\lambda=0.2 lowers three of the four scores by 1.7–2.6 points, so the prediction term must dominate the objective. Halving the batch to 128 changes the scores by at most 0.2 with no consistent sign, and doubling it to 512 lowers them by at most 0.5, so the scores are insensitive to the number of samples per SIGReg estimate in this range; only the smallest batch, 64, costs up to 2.0 on AudioSet-20K.

4.5 Component ablations

Table 7 varies where the regularizer is applied and removes each loss term: “global only” applies the SIGReg term to the global embeddings alone and “local only” to the local embeddings alone, whereas the full objective applies it to both. Restricting the regularizer to either the global or the local embeddings changes the scores by at most one point. Removing either prediction or SIGReg collapses the representation, with all probing scores below 14, so both terms are necessary.

5 Conclusion

We presented MM-LeJEPA, a multimodal extension of LeJEPA that models independent-information and shared-content task components through their gradient moments. Under the stated correspondence and symmetry assumptions, minimizing the weighted Fisher information functional with a fixed total variance yields a correlated Gaussian target. A fixed whitening transform allows this target to be enforced with SIGReg while retaining an objective combining prediction and regularization. This enables multimodal pretraining without reconstruction decoders, contrastive negatives, or an EMA teacher. On public audio-visual classification benchmarks, MM-LeJEPA is competitive with open-source methods under both frozen probing and fine-tuning.

Appendix A Dataset statistics

Appendix B Effect of the target correlation on the embeddings

Figure 2 shows the embeddings of two pretraining runs that differ only in the target correlation ρ\rho, on 1,500 VGGSound test clips; no class labels are used. Each modality on its own (left two columns) looks alike under both settings, so the target correlation does not change the per-modality distribution. In the joint map (third column), the audio and video embeddings of the same clips occupy separate strands for ρ=0\rho=0 and share every small cluster for ρ=0.8\rho=0.8; the fraction of cross-modal nearest neighbors rises from 24% to 46% (50% for fully mixed modalities). The right column plots the paired coordinates (ea,i,ev,i)(e_{a,i},e_{v,i}) over all clips and coordinates, which is the quantity the target covariance constrains: the density is circular for ρ=0\rho=0 and elongated along the diagonal for ρ=0.8\rho=0.8, with a mean per-coordinate correlation of 0.66.

D.2 Role of weighted Fisher information in the two probes (Eq. 3)

Both relations follow the corresponding proofs of Balestriero & LeCun (2025) step by step (lemma and appendix numbers refer to arXiv v3). The task definitions, estimators and regularity conditions below are taken from LeJEPA and restated here to make the appendix self-contained. Our task prior changes only the term involving the second moment of the task gradient, and we expand that term alone. We write KK for the embedding dimension (K=2​dK=2d for the joint embedding) and 𝒦\mathcal{K} for the kernel.

Conditional on η\eta, the training samples 𝒟\mathcal{D} are i.i.d. and independent of 𝐪\mathbf{q}, and we define Bias(𝐪)=𝔼𝒟[y^(𝐪)∣η,𝐪]−η(𝐪)\operatorname{Bias}(\mathbf{q})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\widehat{y}(\mathbf{q})\mid\eta,\mathbf{q}]-\eta(\mathbf{q}) and ISB:=𝔼η,𝐪​[Bias⁡(𝐪)2]\mathrm{ISB}:=\mathbb{E}_{\eta,\mathbf{q}}[\operatorname{Bias}(\mathbf{q})^{2}]. Set zero-denominator predictions to zero; the remainder assumptions include this convention.

Radius-based kk-NN probe: task and estimator.

Following Balestriero & LeCun (2025, Appendix A.1), the embedding density pzp_{z} is C3C^{3} with derivatives of order up to three bounded and with finite Fisher information and covariance. The unknown labels are given by a target function η:ℝK→ℝ\eta:\mathbb{R}^{K}\to\mathbb{R} assumed C2C^{2}; classification is handled by setting η⁡(𝐳)=ℙ⁡(Y=1∣𝐳)\eta(\mathbf{z})=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\mathbf{z}). The training data consist of the NN embeddings together with their labels {(𝐳n,η⁡(𝐳n))}n=1N\{(\mathbf{z}_{n},\eta(\mathbf{z}_{n}))\}_{n=1}^{N}, and we write yn:=η⁡(𝐳n)y_{n}:=\eta(\mathbf{z}_{n}). The prediction at a query 𝐪\mathbf{q} averages the labels of the training points inside a ball of radius r0r_{0},

y^(𝐪):=1Nr0​(𝐪)∑n:‖𝐳n−𝐪‖≤r0yn,\widehat{y}(\mathbf{q}):=\frac{1}{N_{r_{0}}(\mathbf{q})}\sum_{n\,:\,\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{q}\|\leq r_{0}}y_{n}, (19)
Nr0​(𝐪):=#⁡{n:‖𝐳n−𝐪‖≤r0},N_{r_{0}}(\mathbf{q}):=\#\left\{n:\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{q}\|\leq r_{0}\right\}, (20)

where the radius r0r_{0} controls how many neighbors are averaged. Query points follow the training distribution, 𝐪∼pz\mathbf{q}\sim p_{z}.

Following Lemma 4 of Balestriero & LeCun (2025), we write the bias expansion as

The remainder ξr0\xi_{r_{0}} includes finite-sample corrections; we assume 𝔼η,𝐪​[ξr02]=o⁡(r04)\mathbb{E}_{\eta,\mathbf{q}}[\xi_{r_{0}}^{2}]=o(r_{0}^{4}) in the joint large-sample, small-radius limit. Following their notation we abbreviate A(𝐪):=∇η(𝐪)⊤∇logpz(𝐪)A(\mathbf{q}):=\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})^{\top}\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{q}) and C⁡(𝐪):=12​Δ​η​(𝐪)C(\mathbf{q}):=\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\eta(\mathbf{q}). 𝔼η,𝐪​[Bias⁡(𝐪)2]=(r02K+2)2​{𝔼η,𝐪​[A2]⏟score–gradient+2​𝔼η,𝐪​[A​C]⏟cross+𝔼η,𝐪​[C2]⏟curvature}+o⁡(r04).\mathbb{E}_{\eta,\mathbf{q}}\!\left[\operatorname{Bias}(\mathbf{q})^{2}\right]=\left(\frac{r_{0}^{2}}{K+2}\right)^{2}\Big\{\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\eta,\mathbf{q}}\!\left[A^{2}\right]}_{\text{score--gradient}}+2\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\eta,\mathbf{q}}\!\left[AC\right]}_{\text{cross}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\eta,\mathbf{q}}\!\left[C^{2}\right]}_{\text{curvature}}\Big\}+o(r_{0}^{4}). Only the score–gradient term involves the second moment of the task gradient. Expanding this term with the joint prior of Section 3 in place of the isotropic one, and using the identity of Appendix D.1,

=𝔼𝐪tr(∇logpz(𝐪)∇logpz(𝐪)⊤𝔼η[∇η(𝐪)∇η(𝐪)⊤])\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{q}}\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{q})\nabla\log p_{z}(\mathbf{q})^{\top}\,\mathbb{E}_{\eta}\!\left[\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})^{\top}\right]\right)

Following Balestriero & LeCun (2025, Appendix A.2), consider a nonnegative kernel 𝒦:ℝK→ℝ\mathcal{K}:\mathbb{R}^{K}\to\mathbb{R} with the standard properties

ℳ(L,B):={η∈C2(ℝK):‖∇η(𝐪)‖≤L,|Δη(𝐪)|≤B,∀𝐪∈ℝK}.\mathcal{M}(L,B):=\left\{\eta\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{K}):\left\|\nabla\eta(\mathbf{q})\right\|\leq L,\ \left|\Delta\eta(\mathbf{q})\right|\leq B,\ \forall\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}\right\}. (30)

≤(h2​μ2​(𝒦)2)2[2𝔼η∫(Δη)2pz+8𝔼η∫(∇η⊤∇logpz)2pz]+o(h4).\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{h^{2}\mu_{2}(\mathcal{K})}{2}\right)^{2}\left[2{\mathbb{E}_{\eta}}\int\left(\Delta\eta\right)^{2}p_{z}+8{\mathbb{E}_{\eta}}\int\left(\nabla\eta^{\top}\nabla\log p_{z}\right)^{2}p_{z}\right]+o(h^{4}).

D.3 Sources of the isotropic Fisher bound and equality conditions (Eq. 4)

The unweighted Fisher bound and Gaussian equality condition used in Eq. (4) are established in Lemma 6 of Balestriero & LeCun (2025, Appendix B.4, p. 30); the trace-constraint step and its equality condition are given in Step 2(a) of the same appendix. The resulting isotropic Gaussian optimum pz∗=𝒩⁡(0,IK)p_{z}^{*}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{K}) is the trace-constrained case of that appendix’s concluding optimality statement.

Proof of Proposition 1.

By the independent-information conditions of Assumption 2, WindW_{\mathrm{ind}} has diagonal blocks τind2​Id\tau_{\mathrm{ind}}^{2}I_{d} and zero cross blocks. +π⁡(1−π)𝔼η[∇ηind∇ηsame⊤+∇ηsame∇ηind⊤]\displaystyle+\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}\,\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{same}}^{\top}+\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{same}}\nabla\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}^{\top}]

D.5 Proof of Proposition 2 (Eq. 13)

Proof of Proposition 2.

Let pzp_{z} satisfy the conditions of Proposition 2, namely zero mean, covariance Σ=𝔼𝐳∼pz​[𝐳𝐳⊤]≻0\Sigma=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{z}}[\mathbf{z}\mathbf{z}^{\top}]\succ 0, pz∈C3p_{z}\in C^{3} with bounded derivatives up to order three, finite Fisher information and covariance, and pzp_{z} everywhere positive on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d}. Under these conditions, the proof of Lemma 6 of LeJEPA (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025, Appendix B.4) applies the matrix Cramér–Rao bound (Cramér, 1946; Rao, 1945) to the family of shifted densities p𝝁​(𝐳)=pz​(𝐳−𝝁)p_{\bm{\mu}}(\mathbf{z})=p_{z}(\mathbf{z}-\bm{\mu}), whose Fisher information with respect to the shift 𝝁\bm{\mu} is ℐ⁡(pz)\mathcal{I}(p_{z}). It yields ℐ⁡(pz)⪰Σ−1\mathcal{I}(p_{z})\succeq\Sigma^{-1}, with equality if and only if pz=𝒩⁡(0,Σ)p_{z}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma).

Multiplying ℐ⁡(pz)−Σ−1⪰0\mathcal{I}(p_{z})-\Sigma^{-1}\succeq 0 by WAV1/2W_{\mathrm{AV}}^{1/2} on both sides and taking traces,

JWAV​(pz)−tr⁡(WAV​Σ−1)=tr⁡(WAV1/2​(ℐ⁡(pz)−Σ−1)​WAV1/2)≥ 0,J_{W_{\mathrm{AV}}}(p_{z})-\operatorname{tr}\!\left(W_{\mathrm{AV}}\Sigma^{-1}\right)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(W_{\mathrm{AV}}^{1/2}\left(\mathcal{I}(p_{z})-\Sigma^{-1}\right)W_{\mathrm{AV}}^{1/2}\right)\ \geq\ 0, (36)

which is Eq. (13). If Eq. (13) holds with equality, the positive semidefinite matrix WAV1/2​(ℐ⁡(pz)−Σ−1)​WAV1/2W_{\mathrm{AV}}^{1/2}\left(\mathcal{I}(p_{z})-\Sigma^{-1}\right)W_{\mathrm{AV}}^{1/2} has zero trace and is therefore 00. Since WAV≻0W_{\mathrm{AV}}\succ 0, the square root WAV1/2W_{\mathrm{AV}}^{1/2} is invertible, so ℐ⁡(pz)=Σ−1\mathcal{I}(p_{z})=\Sigma^{-1} and the equality condition above gives pz=𝒩⁡(0,Σ)p_{z}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma). Conversely, if pz=𝒩⁡(0,Σ)p_{z}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) then ℐ⁡(pz)=Σ−1\mathcal{I}(p_{z})=\Sigma^{-1} and Eq. (13) holds with equality. ∎
